entry: Cylindrical conformal [[Map projection|map projection]], first presented by Flemish geographer and mapmaker Gerardus Mercator in 1569. Because it represents rhumb lines as straight lines, it became the standard projection for [[Navigation|navigation]] in the 18th century. On world maps it inflates the size of landmasses the farther they are from the [[Equator|equator]], so that [[Greenland]] and [[Antarctica]] appear far larger than landmasses near the equator. Historian Joseph Needham speculated, without evidence, that some [[Song dynasty]] star charts may have been drafted on the projection, but astronomical historian Kazuhiko Miyajima concluded from cartometric analysis that they used an equirectangular projection instead. Its use for maps other than marine charts declined in the 20th century but resurged in the 21st century because of characteristics favorable for online mapping.

German luxury automotive brand, founded in 1926 and commonly called Mercedes. Mercedes-Benz AG, based in [[Stuttgart]], manufactures luxury vehicles and light commercial vehicles. Its roots lie in the 1886 Benz Patent-Motorwagen of [[Carl Benz]], widely recognized as the first automobile powered by an [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]], and in the 1901 Mercedes built by Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft. In 2018 the brand sold 2.31 million passenger cars, making it the world's largest premium vehicle brand.

Watercraft that transports cargo or carries passengers for hire, as distinct from pleasure craft and naval ships. Merchant ships range from 6-meter inflatable dive boats to 300-meter oil tankers and container ships, and include tugboats and passenger-carrying submarines. Many operate under a "flag of convenience" from a country other than the home of their owners, such as Liberia or Panama, whose maritime laws are more favorable. The Greek fleet accounts for some 16 percent of the world's tonnage, making it the largest single international merchant fleet, though not the largest in history. [[Cargo ship|Cargo ships]] handle the bulk of international trade, and bulk carriers move commodities such as iron ore, coal and grain. During wars, merchant ships may serve as auxiliaries to navies and carry military personnel and materiel.

Chemical element with symbol Hg (from Latin *hydrargyrum*), atomic number 80, also known as quicksilver. It is the only metal known to be liquid at standard temperature and pressure, and it has the lowest freezing point, the lowest boiling point and the narrowest liquid range of any metal. Mercury occurs mostly as [[Cinnabar|cinnabar]] (mercuric sulfide), from which the red pigment [[Vermilion|vermilion]] is made. Exposure to mercury and its compounds is toxic to the nervous system, immune system and kidneys. It was long used in [[Thermometer|thermometers]], [[Barometer|barometers]] and other instruments, but concerns about toxicity have reduced its use. It remains in scientific research, in dental [[Amalgam (chemistry)|amalgam]] in some locales and in fluorescent lamps. Its melting point is −38.83 °C and its boiling point 356.73 °C.

Breed or group of breeds of domestic [[Sheep|sheep]], characterized by very fine soft [[Wool|wool]]. It originated in the [[Iberian Peninsula]] during the [[Middle Ages|High Middle Ages]] and was for several centuries a strict Spanish monopoly, with exports forbidden under threat of [[Capital punishment|capital punishment]]. In the 18th century flocks were sent to the courts of France, Hungary, the Netherlands, [[Prussia]], [[Saxony]] and Sweden, and the breed later spread to South America, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. Fiber diameters typically range from 15 to 22 microns. Introduced to Australia in 1797 from Spain's royal flocks, Merinos made the continent the world's premier source of superfine wool. Rams of other Merino breeds have long, spiral horns, while ewes are usually hornless; the Australian Poll Merino is a hornless variant.

Type of plant tissue made up of undifferentiated [[Stem cell|stem cells]] that divide continuously. Meristematic cells are totipotent, able to differentiate into any plant cell type, and they are the source of all differentiated plant tissues and organs. Some remain meristematic while others specialize and usually lose the ability to divide. These cells are small, with thin primary cell walls, few or no vacuoles, dense protoplasm, and proplastids instead of mature [[Plastid|plastids]]. Meristems fall into three main types: apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots, which drive primary growth; intercalary or basal meristems in the middle of stems or leaves, which enable regrowth; and lateral meristems, or [[Vascular cambium|cambium]], which produce secondary growth in woody plants. The term was first used in 1858 by Swiss botanist Carl Wilhelm von Nägeli.

Mythical prophet and magician in the legend of [[King Arthur]]. The familiar figure was introduced by the 12th-century cleric Geoffrey of Monmouth, who made him a prophet and royal advisor to Arthur's father, Uther Pendragon, and combined earlier Welsh tales to form him. His traditional biography makes him a cambion, born of a mortal woman and an [[Incubus|incubus]]. Later stories cast him as a mentor to the young king, who disappears leaving prophecies behind. In a popular French version, he is bewitched and sealed up by the Lady of the Lake.

Legendary aquatic creature with the head and upper body of a woman and the tail of a fish. Mermaids appear in the folklore of many cultures, including those of Europe, Latin America, Asia and Africa, and are sometimes associated with storms, shipwrecks and drownings, though in other traditions they are benevolent. The male counterpart is the merman. The Western image of mermaids as seductive singers may derive from the [[Siren (mythology)|sirens]] of [[Greek mythology]], who were originally half bird; the two became conflated in the [[Middle Ages]]. Reports such as those of [[Christopher Columbus]] off the Caribbean coast may describe [[Manatee|manatees]] or [[Dugong|dugongs]]. Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid" (1837) shaped the modern image, and mermaids continue to appear in art, literature and film. Nineteenth-century "Fiji mermaids" were composite taxidermy hoaxes.

Ancient city on the east bank of the [[Nile]] in northern [[Sudan]], capital of the [[Kingdom of Kush]] for several centuries. The city served as the capital from around 590 BC until the kingdom's collapse in the 4th century AD. King Aspelta moved the capital south from Napata, possibly around 591 BC. Its location lay on the fringe of the summer rainfall belt and near rich deposits of [[Iron|iron]] ore and hardwood for iron working, with access to trade routes to the [[Red Sea]]. The site is marked by more than two hundred [[Pyramid|pyramids]] in three groups, many in ruins, with the distinctive size and proportions of Nubian pyramids. In the 5th century BC, [[Herodotus]] described it as "a great city...said to be the mother city of the other Ethiopians."

Ruling family of the [[Franks]] from around the middle of the 5th century until 751. Under [[Clovis I|Clovis]], who converted to [[Christianity|Nicene Christianity]], the Merovingians united the Franks and conquered most of [[Gaul]], defeating the [[Visigoths]] in 507 and the Burgundians in 534. Their realm was the largest and most powerful state of [[Western Europe]] after the breakup of the empire of [[Theodoric the Great]]. The kingdom was treated as single yet divisible, and Clovis's four sons divided it, with the main divisions Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy and Aquitaine. The kings were called "long-haired kings" because a king whose hair was cut could not rule. In the final century of the dynasty, real power passed to the mayors of the palace, such as [[Charles Martel]], and in 751 Pepin the Short deposed the last king, Childeric III, initiating the Carolingian dynasty.

[[Prime number|Prime number]] of the form 2ⁿ − 1, one less than a power of two. The exponent n must itself be prime, but not every prime exponent gives a prime, as 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 = 23 × 89 shows. The primes are named after the French friar Marin Mersenne, who studied them in the early 17th century. The Euclid–Euler theorem links them to [[Perfect number|even perfect numbers]]. As of 2025, 52 Mersenne primes were known, and all newly found ones since 1997 have come from the distributed Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search. It is not known whether there are infinitely many.

American actress, recognized for her technical precision, command of dialects and professional longevity. Streep began her stage career in 1975 in *Trelawny of the Wells* and was nominated for a Tony Award the following year for *27 Wagons Full of Cotton*. She moved to film with *Julia* (1977), and her first [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nomination followed for *The Deer Hunter* (1978). She won her first Oscar for *Kramer vs. Kramer* (1979), later a second for *Sophie's Choice* (1982) and a third for *The Iron Lady* (2011). She holds the record for the most Golden Globe and Academy Award nominations of any performer, with 34 and 21 respectively. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2014 and is an advocate for gender parity and labor protections.

Isolated, flat-topped elevation bounded on all sides by steep escarpments and standing distinctly above a surrounding [[Plain|plain]]. A mesa consists of flat-lying soft [[Shale|shales]] capped by a resistant layer of harder rock, such as [[Sandstone|sandstone]] or [[Limestone|limestone]], that forms a caprock protecting the flat summit. Unlike a [[Plateau|plateau]], which may lack horizontal bedrock, as with the [[Tibetan Plateau]], a mesa is defined by flat-lying strata and steep-sided isolation. A butte is a smaller, eroded mesa with a limited summit, while a cuesta has a gentle dip slope and one steep escarpment because its strata are tilted. Large, flat-topped plateaus with horizontal strata are called tablelands.

Naturally occurring psychedelic alkaloid found in certain [[Cactus|cacti]], such as peyote and the San Pedro cactus. Chemically 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenethylamine, it acts mainly as a partial agonist at [[Serotonin|serotonin]] 5-HT2A receptors. Psychedelic effects occur at oral doses of 100 to 800 mg of its hydrochloride salt. Mescaline was first synthesized in 1919 and has been called the "first psychedelic." It is largely illegal worldwide, with exceptions for religious, scientific or ornamental use. It has influenced figures such as [[Aldous Huxley]].

Building traditions of pre-Columbian [[Mesoamerica]], best known from public, ceremonial and urban monumental structures. Its pyramids are the largest such structures outside [[Ancient Egypt]]. Many features were governed by religious and mythological ideas, and the layout of most cities was influenced by the [[Cardinal direction|cardinal directions]] and their symbolic meanings. Monumental buildings were decorated with religious images and, in some cases, writing. From about 1800 BCE until the Spanish conquest of the 16th century, builders used stone, stucco and earth, without metal tools or the wheel, to create stepped pyramids, ball courts, palaces and plazas. The [[Teotihuacan]] megacity, with over 100,000 inhabitants, featured the Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon. Maya city-states such as [[Tikal]] built corbelled arches and multi-level temples, while the Aztec capital [[Tenochtitlan]] was a floating city on Lake Texcoco.

Archaeological period of the Old World between the [[Upper Paleolithic]] and the [[Neolithic]], also called the Middle Stone Age. It denotes the final period of [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherer]] cultures in Europe and the Middle East, between the end of the [[Last Glacial Maximum]] and the [[Neolithic Revolution]]. In Europe it spans roughly 15,000 to 5,000 years before present; in the Middle East, roughly 20,000 to 10,000. It is associated with a shift from group hunting of large animals to a broader foraging way of life, with smaller, more sophisticated stone tools, including microliths hafted into composite weapons. Settlements were often near the sea or inland waters, and diets included wild game, fish, shellfish and nuts. Some sites show early use of pottery. Agriculture marks the transition to the Neolithic.

[[Hadron|Hadronic]] subatomic particle composed of an equal number of [[Quark|quarks]] and antiquarks, usually one of each, bound together by the [[Strong interaction|strong interaction]]. Mesons are about one femtometer in diameter (10⁻¹⁵ m), roughly 0.6 times the size of a [[Proton|proton]] or neutron, and all are unstable. Outside the nucleus they appear only briefly, as products of very high-energy collisions such as those of cosmic rays, and they are routinely produced in particle accelerators. Conventional two-quark mesons are [[Boson|bosons]], whereas [[Baryon|baryons]] are fermions. Each meson has an antiparticle; the positive [[Pion|pion]] is made of an up quark and a down antiquark. The heavier J/psi, first seen in 1974, is about three times as massive as a proton.

Cancer developing from the mesothelium, the thin tissue layer that covers many internal organs. It most often affects the lining of the lungs and chest wall. Symptoms may include shortness of breath, a swollen abdomen, chest wall pain and weight loss. More than 80 percent of cases are caused by [[Asbestos|asbestos]] exposure, usually about 40 years earlier. Diagnosis relies on imaging and a tissue [[Biopsy|biopsy]], and treatment often combines surgery, radiation therapy and [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]]. The five-year survival rate in the United States averages eight percent.

Era of Earth's geological history lasting from about 252 to 66 million years ago, comprising the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. It began after the [[Permian–Triassic extinction event]], the largest mass extinction in Earth's history, and ended with the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]], which killed the non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs, mosasaurs and plesiosaurs. Known as the Age of the Dinosaurs, it saw dinosaurs become the dominant terrestrial vertebrates by the Late Triassic or Early Jurassic. The supercontinent [[Pangaea]] began to break apart, and the climate was generally hotter than today. The first mammals appeared but remained smaller than 15 kg until the [[Cenozoic]]. [[Flowering plant|Flowering plants]] appeared in the Early Cretaceous and rapidly diversified, replacing conifers and other gymnosperms as the dominant plants.

Savior or liberator of a group of people in [[Abrahamic religions]]. The concept originated in [[Judaism]] and the [[Hebrew Bible]], where a *mashiach* ("anointed one") was a king, prophet or high priest anointed with holy oil. In Judaism, the Messiah is expected to be a human descendant of King David through an unbroken paternal line, who will unify the tribes of Israel, rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem and usher in a global Messianic Age of peace. [[Christians]] regard [[Jesus]] as the Messiah, believing that Old Testament prophecies were fulfilled in his mission, death and resurrection, and that he will return at the [[Second Coming|second coming]]. In [[Islam]], Jesus is held to be a prophet and the Messiah sent to the Israelites, who will return with the Mahdi to defeat the false Messiah, al-Masih ad-Dajjal.

English-language oratorio by German-born Baroque composer [[George Frideric Handel]], composed in 1741. Charles Jennens compiled its text from the King James Bible and the Coverdale Psalter. It was first performed in [[Dublin]] on 13 April 1742 and received its London premiere a year later, becoming one of the best-known choral works in Western music. It is not dramatic: Part I begins with prophecies by [[Isaiah]] and moves to the annunciation to the shepherds, Part II concentrates on the Passion of [[Jesus]] and ends with the "Hallelujah" chorus, and Part III covers the resurrection of the dead. Handel wrote it for modest forces, but later performances used giant orchestras and choirs of up to 800 performers. Efforts to update its orchestration began with [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart|Mozart]]'s *Der Messias*. The autograph manuscript is preserved in the [[British Library]].

Supergiant [[Elliptical galaxy|elliptical galaxy]] in the constellation Virgo, also known as Virgo A or NGC 4486. It contains several trillion stars and is one of the largest and most massive galaxies in the local universe. It has about 15,000 globular clusters, compared with 150 to 200 orbiting the [[Milky Way]]. A jet of energetic plasma extends at least 4,900 light-years from its core at a relativistic speed. Charles Messier discovered it in 1781 and cataloged it as a nebula. It lies about 53 million light-years from Earth and is the second-brightest galaxy in the northern [[Virgo Cluster]]. Its core holds an active [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]], which forms the primary component of an [[Active galactic nucleus|active galactic nucleus]]. The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the black hole using data collected in 2017, with the image released on 10 April 2019.

Deep-sky object listed in the catalog compiled by French astronomer Charles Messier. Messier, who sought [[Comet|comets]], listed the non-comet objects that frustrated his search. The catalog was compiled with his assistant Pierre Méchain and was eventually expanded to 110 objects. It includes star clusters, nebulae and galaxies such as the [[Andromeda Galaxy]] (M31), and covers most deep-sky objects visible from the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. Messier 1 is the [[Crab Nebula]]. Many of the objects are popular targets for amateur astronomers.

Spanish term for a person of mixed ancestry, usually Spanish and Indigenous American. The term originated as a formal label for the mixed-race [[Caste|castas]] of the [[Spanish Empire]], used in censuses, parish registers and [[Inquisition]] trials. With the Bourbon reforms and independence, the caste system disappeared and the term fell out of favor. In much of [[Latin America]] it later became a cultural term, while indio was reserved for people who kept a separate Indigenous identity. In Mexico it became central to national identity after the [[Mexican Revolution]].

Statistical method for combining quantitative results from multiple independent studies of a common research question. Analysts compute a combined effect size across the studies, which increases statistical power and can resolve discrepancies among individual studies. Meta-analyses are often part of a systematic review and help shape treatment guidelines and health policies. The technique emerged in the social sciences in the 1970s, and the term was coined in 1976 by psychologist Gene V. Glass. It is used in medicine, psychology, education and ecology. Common models assume either a single true effect or variation between studies, and results are often displayed in forest plots. Challenges include [[Bias|publication bias]], which favors statistically significant findings, and the combination of heterogeneous studies.
